title: How to Reindustrialize America
gist: Former U.S. National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan argues that China's 1,700-plus state 'guidance funds' (~$700bn) have produced an industrial-innovation ecosystem the U.S. cannot match with markets alone, and proposes a federally chartered $50 billion Strategic Investment Fund plus a cabinet-level Strategic Investment Council to combine public co-investment, multiyear offtake, targeted tariffs and permitting relief in advanced computing, biotech, robotics, critical minerals, pharma precursors, advanced manufacturing and the electric-energy backbone.

themes.theme: Second China Shock at the Tech Frontier

insights.claim: The next China shock to the United States will be a contest for technological primacy across AI, quantum computing, aerospace, next-generation energy and biotechnology rather than a wave of cheap exports.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Frames China risk as competition in high-margin frontier sectors, not just import price pressure — the exposure sits in U.S. tech and capital-goods leaders, not only in low-end manufacturing.
insights.quote: a “second China shock,” not of cheap exports, but of technological primacy
insights.locator: For more than a century, America’s unmatched ability

insights.claim: China's state-tilted capital allocation lets its firms overbuild capacity and flood markets before American and allied competitors can scale production, structurally disadvantaging Western entrants even when they hold the technology lead.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Expect recurring price collapses in any sector Beijing targets; Western capex in those verticals needs policy protection to earn a return.
insights.locator: The result is a market systematically tilted

insights.claim: China has twice used rare-earth export restrictions as coercive leverage — against Japan in 2010 over the East China Sea islands dispute and against the United States fifteen years later, the latter forcing President Trump to scale back triple-digit tariffs on Chinese goods.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Rare-earth export controls are a proven de-escalation lever for Beijing — tariff policy is hostage to minerals dependence, a repeatable trade-war pattern.
insights.locator: In 2010, China cut rare-earth exports to Japan

insights.claim: Industrial capacity has become an instrument of coercion, not merely of competitiveness, in Chinese statecraft.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Supply-chain concentration should be priced as geopolitical option value held by Beijing, not just as a cost advantage.
insights.quote: For China, industrial capacity has become a tool of coercion as well as competitiveness.
insights.locator: For China, industrial capacity has become

insights.claim: Chinese provinces, cities and national ministries have created more than 1,700 'guidance funds' raising nearly $700 billion, professionally managed and profit-seeking vehicles that direct equity into priority sectors alongside state-provided land and permits.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Sets the benchmark scale any U.S. or allied industrial-finance response must be measured against — a $50bn U.S. fund is an order of magnitude smaller.
insights.quote: have created more than 1,700 “guidance funds,” raising nearly $700 billion in capital
insights.locator: China has built a comprehensive system of state-guided investment

insights.claim: China's decentralized guidance-fund model generates immense duplication and waste yet still produces globally dominant national champions including CATL in batteries, LONGi in solar, DJI in drones and Huawei in telecommunications.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Waste-tolerant capital is a feature, not a bug — Western critiques of Chinese overcapacity miss that the surviving champions capture the global market.
insights.locator: The approach has generated immense duplication and waste

insights.claim: Shenzhen manufactured demand for BYD by mandating electrification of its bus and taxi fleets, giving the then-emerging EV maker guaranteed demand, stable cash flow and real-world engineering feedback that private markets could not supply.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Public fleet mandates are the cheapest known accelerant for a hardware champion — watch for U.S. and allied procurement mandates as the leading indicator of who scales next.
insights.locator: Take Shenzhen’s promotion of electric vehicles

insights.claim: BYD has surpassed Tesla in global unit sales and China has overtaken Japan as the world's largest auto exporter.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Concrete scoreboard evidence that the industrial-commons model beats a single-firm innovation model in autos; Japanese and U.S. OEM export share is the structural loser.
insights.quote: BYD has since surpassed Tesla in global unit sales, and China has overtaken Japan as the world’s largest auto exporter.
insights.locator: BYD has since surpassed Tesla

insights.claim: China is converting manufacturing know-how back into frontier innovation gains in sectors the United States traditionally dominated, including biotechnology.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Chinese biotech is a rising competitive threat to U.S. pharma's discovery franchise, not just a low-cost CRO supplier.
insights.locator: At the same time, China is converting the knowledge

themes.theme: American Chokepoints and Lost Process Knowledge

insights.claim: Nearly 700 U.S.-approved medicines, including critical antibiotics, depend on at least one chemical produced solely in China.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Pharmaceutical precursor onshoring is a named priority sector — chemical and API reshoring plays have policy tailwinds.
insights.quote: nearly 700 U.S.-approved medicines, including critical drugs such as antibiotics, depend on at least one chemical produced solely in China
insights.locator: In pharmaceuticals, nearly 700 U.S.-approved medicines

insights.claim: The world's dependence on Taiwan for the most advanced chips constitutes a single and fragile point of failure for the global economy.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Reinforces the policy bid under U.S.-sited leading-edge fabs regardless of near-term economics.
insights.locator: The world relies on Taiwan for production

insights.claim: A scarcity of American dry docks limits U.S. naval readiness and dependence on imported power transformers has slowed national grid upgrades while leaving the grid exposed to prolonged outages.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Transformers, shipyards and grid hardware are explicitly flagged for multiyear federal purchasing commitments — a visible demand pipeline for those manufacturers.
insights.locator: A scarcity of American dry docks

insights.claim: The United States has allowed its 'electric tech stack' — the linked supply chains for critical minerals, batteries, power electronics and chips — to drift offshore, weakening industrial learning and depth.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Treats minerals-to-chips as one integrated stack; policy support is likely to be awarded stack-wide rather than to isolated firms.
insights.locator: While China builds tightly clustered ecosystems

insights.claim: In complex, high-value industries innovation depends on physical proximity between design and production, so offshoring manufacturing breaks the feedback loops between engineers and factory floors and degrades invention itself.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
entities: Task Force on Production in the Innovation Economy
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'design here, build there' asset-light model — argues long-run R&D productivity of offshored firms decays.
insights.locator: MIT’s Task Force on Production in the Innovation Economy

insights.claim: U.S. shipbuilding collapsed after the 1980s when government subsidies were withdrawn, erasing supplier depth and design expertise, demonstrating that once production ecosystems fragment they are exceedingly hard to rebuild.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Hysteresis in industrial ecosystems means reshoring costs far exceed the original subsidy saved — argues for paying up early in any targeted sector.
insights.locator: U.S. shipbuilding, for example, collapsed after the 1980s

themes.theme: Why Deep U.S. Capital Markets Still Underfund Factories

insights.claim: American capital markets optimize for efficiency rather than resilience or security, so the core policy challenge is turning capital into capability.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: The stated diagnosis behind the whole proposal — expect policy to target the efficiency-resilience gap with subsidized risk capital rather than with deregulation alone.
insights.locator: But those markets optimize for efficiency

insights.claim: Nuclear plants, semiconductor fabs, shipyards, transformer factories and rare-earth refineries require upfront capital and decade-long horizons that a single shift in tariffs, procurement rules, grid standards or commodity prices can wipe out, making individually rational investor caution produce collective underinvestment.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Policy certainty — offtake contracts, stable rules, price floors — is the actual unlock; watch for price-floor mechanisms as the signal that private capital will follow.
insights.locator: First, some strategic industrial sectors depend on conditions

insights.claim: The United States has a structural financing gap at the scale-up stage between venture funding and public markets, because local banks that financed regional producers have disappeared and venture investors avoid asset-heavy factory capital as too slow for venture-level returns.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
entities: Production in the Innovation Economy Task Force
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific capital-structure niche public money would occupy — growth-stage hardware debt, a segment private credit is also moving into.
insights.locator: Next, research by the Production in the Innovation Economy Task Force

insights.claim: Markets systematically fail to value the positive externalities of strategic physical industries — learning-by-doing, supplier networks and engineering capability — because no single firm can capture those spillovers.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: The economic justification for subsidy; implies public support is durable across administrations only if framed as externality correction rather than favoritism.
insights.locator: Finally, markets fail to value positive externalities

insights.claim: A U.S. manufacturing CEO described raising domestic capital for first-of-a-kind technology as a series of near-death experiences that was then undercut by state-subsidized Chinese copycats with free land and guaranteed buyers.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Illustrates why U.S. hardware startups fail even when technically ahead — fast-follower risk from subsidized rivals is the dominant terminal-value risk.
insights.quote: raising U.S. capital for his first-of-a-kind technology was a series of near-death experiences—one that was quickly undercut by a flood of copycat Chinese competitors propped up by state subsidies, free land, and guaranteed buyers
insights.locator: As one innovative U.S. manufacturing CEO told me

insights.claim: In nuclear energy and mineral processing the binding constraint is often not capital at all but prohibitive soft costs from a disjointed permitting and regulatory landscape that consumes years of capital while creating no tangible value.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Money without permitting reform will not move these projects — permitting timelines are the variable to track for nuclear and minerals developers.
insights.locator: Yet the hurdle for American industry is as much a fragmented state at home

themes.theme: Hamiltonian Precedent: RFC, DPC and Cold War Procurement

insights.claim: The Reconstruction Finance Corporation's wartime subsidiary, the Defense Plant Corporation, built more than 2,000 factories and shipyards and transferred them to private operators, creating the foundation of postwar American dominance in steel, aviation and chemicals.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: The historical template being invoked — build-and-transfer to private operators, not permanent state ownership; sets expectations for how a new fund would exit.
insights.locator: Its wartime subsidiary, the Defense Plant Corporation

insights.claim: Government procurement created the U.S. semiconductor industry: the Air Force's Minuteman program and NASA's Apollo missions bought thousands of chips when no private buyer would, driving costs down until Fairchild, Intel, AMD and Micron could build a commercial ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: The precedent argument for guaranteed public offtake as an industry-creating tool — the same logic now being applied to nuclear, storage and transformers.
insights.locator: Early defense- and space-related procurement of semiconductors

insights.claim: From the mid-1970s inflation and energy shocks eroded confidence in federal industrial policy, narrowing Washington's remit from investor to regulator through the 1980s and 1990s and atrophying the connective tissue between research, finance and production.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Positions the current industrial-policy turn as a fifty-year regime change in the state's economic role — a durable macro regime, not a one-cycle stimulus.
insights.locator: By the mid-1970s, however, the broader political and economic consensus

insights.claim: Federal industrial action to date has been reactive and crisis-driven — COVID-era emergency authorities for medical supplies, post-Ukraine munitions and solid-rocket-motor interventions, and Defense Production Act invocations for rare-earth processing and permanent magnets — leaving it episodic and vulnerable to reversal across administrations.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Political-risk warning: current supply-chain support programs are reversible, so contracts tied to emergency authorities carry administration-change risk.
insights.locator: Because the United States lacks such a framework

themes.theme: Strategic Investment Fund Design and Governance

insights.claim: The proposed U.S. Strategic Investment Fund would launch with $50 billion — comparable to the CHIPS and Science Act but with a broader mandate — deploying attractive financing, credit guarantees, convertible debt and equity-like securities so taxpayers share the upside.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: A concrete legislative ask to watch; guarantees and converts, not grants, means the mechanism is designed to crowd in private lenders rather than displace them.
insights.quote: The SIF would launch with $50 billion—comparable to the CHIPS and Science Act but with a broader mandate
insights.locator: The SIF would launch with $50 billion

insights.claim: A cabinet-level Strategic Investment Council chaired by Treasury, including Commerce, Defense, Energy, State and the USTR, would align procurement, targeted tariffs, tax incentives, regulation and credit programs behind common industrial objectives.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Signals a future in which tariffs and subsidies are bundled per-transaction — sector policy would arrive as packages, not isolated tariff headlines.
insights.locator: To create a coherent strategic finance strategy

insights.claim: The council would organize multiyear purchasing commitments from the Defense Department and other agencies for shipbuilding, grid transformers and long-duration energy storage to make otherwise unfinanceable projects bankable.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Names the three asset classes most likely to receive guaranteed federal demand — directly relevant to order-book visibility for those suppliers.
insights.locator: The council would also organize multiyear purchasing commitments

insights.claim: The fund would be governed by a majority-independent board drawn from finance, industry and labor with a Senate-confirmed private-sector chief executive on a fixed term, with every transaction disclosed, audited and bound by portfolio-level return targets.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Governance design is the political precondition for passage; portfolio-level return targets imply commercial pricing discipline on any co-investment.
insights.locator: The SIF would be governed by a professional board

insights.claim: Sector selection would follow economic historian Chris Miller's tests: whether a product can be monopolized for geopolitical leverage, whether U.S. capacity could withstand a crisis, and whether today's ecosystem is necessary to develop tomorrow's.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: A screenable rubric for guessing which sectors get public capital next — monopolizable inputs with crisis relevance rank highest.
insights.locator: To maintain focus, the SIF would lead a systematic

insights.claim: For mature, competitively undifferentiated capital-intensive sectors such as shipbuilding and basic battery cells, the fund would restore baseline capacity with joint ventures, targeted tariffs, multiyear offtake, guarantees and time-limited tax credits, then step back as commercial capital takes over.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Support in commoditized sectors is explicitly designed to be temporary — models assuming permanent subsidy in cells or shipyards overstate the terminal margin.
insights.locator: For capital-intensive industries such as shipbuilding

insights.claim: In innovation-led sectors — advanced robotics, next-generation nuclear power, energy storage, biotech and advanced materials — the highest leverage for flexible public capital is bridging the chasm between prototype and production.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Identifies where public dollars would go first in growth equity terms: pre-commercial hardware companies with proven prototypes needing first-plant financing.
insights.locator: Innovation-led sectors, such as advanced robotics

insights.claim: Following the CHIPS Act precedent of funding TSMC and Samsung, the fund would finance trusted foreign firms building capacity on U.S. soil to accelerate know-how transfer and embed allied producers in the American industrial base, particularly in shipbuilding.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Allied shipbuilders — notably Korean and Japanese yards — are candidates for U.S. subsidized joint ventures, a route into an otherwise closed market.
insights.locator: The fund’s reach would not stop at U.S. firms

insights.claim: Allies have already built comparable vehicles: the United Kingdom's $37 billion National Wealth Fund launched in 2024 to crowd in private capital for infrastructure and energy security, and Australia's $16 billion Future Made in Australia anchored by $9.5 billion in production tax credits for hydrogen and critical mineral refining.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Concrete allied capital pools already deployable into hydrogen and minerals refining — a funding source for projects outside U.S. programs.
insights.locator: Several allied governments have already begun addressing

insights.claim: Without an institutional vehicle to coordinate investment, procurement and trade policy, allies fragment markets and duplicate subsidies and cannot muster the scale to compete with China's state-backed system, which is why ad hoc investment 'funds' shoehorned into trade deals with Japan and South Korea are inadequate.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: A direct critique of the current trade-deal-linked investment pledges — treat those headline fund commitments as unlikely to produce coordinated capacity.
insights.locator: Finally, the United States has no institutional vehicle

themes.theme: Rebutting the Corruption and Boondoggle Objections

insights.claim: The corruption risk in a sovereign investment fund is real but is inherent to executive power rather than unique to the fund, so the answer is structural political independence — an independent-majority board, published criteria and disclosed, audited transactions.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Acknowledges the strongest objection; the credibility of any actual U.S. fund will hinge on whether these guardrails survive the legislative process.
insights.locator: Opponents of a sovereign investment fund might object

insights.claim: Fear of failure following Solyndra's bankruptcy chilled U.S. public investment for over a decade, but competing with China requires accepting that some ventures will fail and judging the portfolio rather than individual deals.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: A deliberate shift in the political risk tolerance for public capital — expect more, and more failure-prone, government-backed hardware bets.
insights.quote: Competing with China requires accepting that some unsuccessful ventures will be inevitable.
insights.locator: Others might frame public investment in emerging technology

insights.claim: Tax credits and tariffs are insufficient substitutes for a strategic fund because credits lower marketwide costs without covering first-of-a-kind risks such as uncertain demand and permitting delays, while tariffs create breathing room but can shelter incumbents without spurring new investment if overused.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: An explicit warning from a former NSA that tariff-led industrial policy alone will not rebuild capacity — a bearish read on tariff-only reshoring theses.
insights.locator: Those more amenable to public strategic finance in principle

insights.claim: The fund would intervene only at the adventurous margin where private capital remains hesitant despite available incentives, structuring its capital as risk-absorbing financing that unlocks rather than replaces private investment.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Implies subordinated or first-loss public tranches — attractive senior economics for private co-investors in strategic projects.
insights.locator: Still others opposed to government intervention in markets

insights.claim: The central question China's rise poses is whether open, market-based democracies can still mobilize capital to serve national ends, and the United States lacks not markets or entrepreneurs but modern instruments to align them with long-term national aims.
insights.speaker: Jake Sullivan
insights.so_what: Frames industrial finance as a bipartisan regime question — the direction of travel toward state-directed capital is likely to persist across administrations.
insights.locator: That imagination is sorely needed today
